context.guidance: Make the erasure route delete the Personal Data Elements from every store, cache and backup in scope, rather than setting a flag or hiding the records. Include the Data Processors in each erasure request, as §8(7)(b) requires, and confirm completion for each one. Keep only what a legal retention duty obliges you to keep, and erase the rest on request under §12(3).

value.fix: Don't stop at `deletionRequested: true` in the erasure handler. Setting a flag or soft-deleting the record is not erasure. The handler should permanently delete or irreversibly anonymise the principal's personal data in every store in scope: primary DB tables, read replicas, caches (e.g. Redis/CDN), search indexes, analytics/log stores and backups. For backups that can't be edited, either expire the data on a short, documented rotation or use crypto-shredding, which deletes the per-user encryption key. Send the erasure request to every Data Processor that holds the data (§8(7)(b)), via its API or DPA channel, and record a confirmation of completion from each one. Before erasing, check each data element against a retention-policy map. Keep only the fields a specific legal duty requires (e.g. tax or accounting records), store them separately with restricted access, and set a deletion date when that duty ends. Erase everything else on request (§12(3)). Keep an audit record (request ID, timestamp, stores purged, processor confirmations, fields retained and the legal basis) that holds no erased personal data. Report the request as complete only when every store and processor has confirmed. Add a test that runs an erasure and then checks the DB, cache, search index and processor stubs for any remaining records.
